subject: Estimating transition probabilities for migratory animals

messages.author: 10e17346e14a0eac
messages.subject: Estimating transition probabilities for migratory animals
parts:
I'm trying to estimate population-level transition probabilities for migratory animals (an aspect of migratory connectivity) from a variety of data sources. I've got several data sources implemented using a bootstrapping approach (see https://github.com/SMBC-NZP/MigConnectivity), and I'm working now on Bayesian implementations. One of the simplest data types has got me stymied, for some reason. That data type is individual-level probabilities of connecting to each of the target populations (e.g., probabilities of breeding population assignment from nonbreeding genetic samples, where one is trying to estimate nonbreeding to breeding population-level transition probabilities). It seems like it should be easy - the data (probT) and parameter to be estimated (psi) are essentially the same thing, transition probabilities to target populations that sum to 1, either by individual or by origin population. But so far everything I've tried either doesn't work at all or gives very biased estimates with simulated data. This is the closest version I'm come up with so far (JAGS code):
model{
# likelihood
for(i in 1:nProbT){
  probT[i, 1:ndest] ~ ddirich(alpha[i, 1:ndest])
  dest[i] ~ dcat(psi[assO[i], 1:ndest])
  for (k in 1:ndest){
    alpha[i, k] <- alphaPrior[i, k] + (dest[i]==k)
  }#k
}#i

# priors
for(j in 1:npop){
  for(k in 1:ndest){
    m0[j, k] ~ dgamma(1, 1)
    psi[j, k] <- m0[j, k] / sum(m0[j, 1:ndest])
  } #k
}#j
}

where nProbT is the number of samples, ndest is the number of target populations, assO is the known origin population for each sampled animal, alphaPrior is all ones (what number I use doesn't seem to matter, unless I use all zeros, in which case I get an error), and npop is the number of origin populations. As I said, this produces very biased psi estimates (much more than the bootstrapping approach with the same data). The direction of this bias is towards making all the psis identical.

Can someone suggest a better approach?

Thank you very much,

Jeff
Jeffrey A. Hostetler, PhD
US Fish and Wildlife Service
Division of Migratory Bird Management
Branch of Assessment and Decision Support

messages.author: ea29cead5e3b8075
messages.subject: Re: Estimating transition probabilities for migratory animals
parts:
Hey Jeff, 

What about something like this? Where 'genetics' is a frequency matrix that represents the number of samples associated with each non-breeding location from each breeding area with nProbT now representing the total number of samples from a specific breeding area. It wasn't clear if 'dest' was actually data or a latent state, but if it's data (i.e., observations of marked birds from a specific breeding area on a specific non-breeding area), this approach would allow both sources of data (genetics and observations) to jointly estimate the same parameter (psi).

for(k in 1: npop ){
  genetics[k,1:ndest) ~ dmulti(psi[k,1:ndest, nProbT[k])

# priors
for(j in 1:npop){
  for(k in 1:ndest){
     m0[j, k] ~ dgamma(1, 1)
     psi[j, k] <- m0[j, k] / sum(m0[j, 1:ndest])
  } #k
}#j

I've done something similar with just observations of birds (no genetic data) and it seemed to work well enough. So, I'd be surprised if this wouldn't work in the absence of a major discrepancy between the two data types.

-Dan

messages.subject: Re: Estimating transition probabilities for migratory animals
parts:
Hi Dan,

Thank you for the suggestion! Apologies for the lack of clarity - dest was put in that version as a latent state to link together psi and probT. Your suggestion is good where we know the target population of individual animals (e.g., telemetry data), but with the genetics data we have at best a table of probabilities, with a row for each animal, and each row summing to 1. Often one of those probabilities is quite high, but I want to incorporate the underlying uncertainty.

Jeff
